item.title: Unions call off bus and regional train strikes for two weeks
item.description:
Unions call off bus and regional train strikes for two weeks

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Unions FNV and CNV have suspended their weekly strikes in regional public transport for two weeks after employers made new commitments on a collective labour agreement, broadcaster NOS reported on Wednesday.

The suspension means Thursday’s planned strike did not go ahead, the unions said in a press release.

The unions announced in early October they would strike one day a week after talks broke down. Staff at operators including Arriva, Keolis and Qbuzz walked out for the first time last week, cancelling many buses and regional trains across the country.

The unions are demanding a 9.5% pay rise over two years and better conditions for older staff.

item.title: Gambling regulator hits illegal casino with record €37m fine
item.description:
Gambling regulator hits illegal casino with record €37m fine

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch gambling regulator KSA has issued a record fine of €37 million on a company for running a dozen unlicensed online casinos.

EOD Code SRL, which says it is registered in Costa Rica, offered games to players in the Netherlands through sites including Instantcasino and Skyhills without a Dutch licence, KSA said on Thursday.

KSA inspectors were able to register and gamble on the sites with no measures in place to stop people in the Netherlands using them. Several of the sites had no visible age checks and accepted cryptocurrency and other anonymous payment methods.

The investigation began with Instantcasino and later uncovered 11 more sites run by the same company. The KSA based the fine on an estimate of the company’s Dutch revenue.

Online gambling was legalised in October 2021, with the government arguing a regulated market would draw players away from illegal sites. But the KSA estimated last year that more money goes to unlicensed sites than to legal ones.

In August, radio station BNR found that illegal operators were targeting Facebook and Instagram ads at people on Cruks, the national register that bars them from gambling. The cabinet set out plans in June to ban online gambling advertising and bonuses.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s use of alcohol, drugs, or gambling, the Jellinek addiction helpline can be reached on 088 505 1220 or at jellinek.nl. The line is staffed in Dutch and English on weekdays, 1pm to 5pm.

item.title: Airbnb to hosts: no more asking guests to wash the dishes
item.description:
Airbnb to hosts: no more asking guests to wash the dishes

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

In addition to increasingly strict rules for hosts renting out their homes on Airbnb – including limits on the number of nights, guest caps and permit fees – there are now new rules to abide by: they can’t ask their guests to do the dishes or remove bed sheets.

Airbnb introduced a new policy on house rules earlier this week that will go into effect on November 20, 2026. Among them are what the company considers “reasonable requests”, which Airbnb defines per chore.

“You may not ask guests to wash everything and store the dishes, but you may ask them to put the dishes in the sink,” says the site.

“You may not ask guests to pick up the bed linen or put the laundry in the washing machine, but you may ask them to collect used towels.”

And: “You may not ask guests to take the garbage and dispose of it elsewhere, but you may ask them to separate their residual waste and recyclable waste in the designated waste bins in the accommodation.”

But “reasonable” appears to be a relative term. Airbnb will let hosts, for example, ask guests to put their garbage in animal-resistant containers if there are bears in the area.

“It’s ridiculous,” said one former Airbnb host who doesn’t want to be named. “The rules were changing all the time, getting more restrictive, which made it increasingly hard to make any money at all. I’m glad I got out of it before I can’t tell my guests to clean up after themselves. What’s next? Will we have to provide sunbeds for them?”

According to the booking website, the world’s largest for private stays, landlords already charge their guests a cleaning fee. Making them clean more is unfair, says Airbnb, and leads to guest dissatisfaction.

Airbnb has faced criticism for years in many cities where it operates, with detractors saying it leads to higher rents, less housing for locals and less livable neighbourhoods, especially in smaller cities with huge tourist populations like Amsterdam and Barcelona.

item.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
item.description:
Partner content

Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague

October 22, 2026

The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. Tickets go for €6 online, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres
Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work
For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health
The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

item.title: Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths
item.description:
Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Thirty websites were taken offline and three men arrested earlier this week in connection to sites that sold counterfeit pills that led to the deaths of three people.

The suspects – a 35-year-old man from Kwintsheul, a 39-year-old man from Rotterdam and a 66-year-old male from The Hague – are suspected of “offering, selling and supplying illegal drugs”, including sedatives, sleeping pills and painkillers like oxycodone, which contained extremely potent synthetic opioids known as nitazenes.

Nitazenes can be many times stronger than morphine and more lethal than fentanyl.

Police say the victims bought the prescription-only pills on websites Slaappillen.net or regionapp.net shortly before they died, and are holding the suspects responsible for running them.

Whack-a-mole

Even though Slaappillen.net was taken down last year, police say the men continued to sell the counterfeit drugs through other websites, which kept popping up as soon as others were taken down.

But according to police, this time they not only took the web shops offline, but confiscated the servers they ran on.

“We have taken down the entire technology behind the websites,” Ron van Brussel told NOS. He is responsible for tackling serious organized crime at the National Investigation and Interventions Unit. “This makes it more difficult to make a restart.”

Both the servers and data have been seized for investigation, and more arrests have not been ruled out.

The police searches were carried out in five locations, including homes and a storage box in The Hague. Crypto wallets, cash and valuables were seized.

With this week’s arrests, police say the main players from the group are now in custody. But, they add, the sale of illegal drugs is far from over.

“There are several criminal groups that keep these types of sites online,” said Van Brussel.

item.title: Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?
item.description:
Partner content

Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?

October 22, 2026

New to the Netherlands or a longer-term resident looking to get your finances organised to make the most of your Dutch life? A little planning, a few local habits and some expert coaching will soon have you in the best financial shape.

The foundation of any fitness plan is the basics, so first of all you need to establish what your monthly costs are likely to be. Alongside your rent or mortgage repayments, you’ll have to pay for health insurance, council taxes, public transport, gas and electricity, and perhaps a gym membership.

“If you are financially fit, you are able to meet all your monthly and annual payments, save some money and live the life you would like to have at that moment,” says Ame Pots, a financial health coach with ABN Amro who helps expats make the most of their money.

What costs can you expect?

ABN Amro is hosting a free webinar on October 28 to explain how to get financially fit in the Netherlands. 

You will have to pay for insurance. Health insurance, for example, will cost you upwards of €160 a month from next year, and you will have to pay the first €400 of insured treatment. You can cut the monthly premium by around €25 if you raise your voluntary deductible by €500, but that means you’ll need to increase your savings so you can pay if you do fall ill. If you want supplementary insurance, such as dental coverage or extra physiotherapy, you will pay more.

By the way, the six-week window for changing health insurer kicks off in mid-November, so now might be a good time to start shopping around for a better deal.

You’ll also have to pay your local authority for waste collection and the water board for water usage. How much you pay depends on the size of your home and how many people live there, but between €250 and €450 a year is the norm in most places. If you are a homeowner, you will pay slightly more. These bills often arrive at the same time of year, in the spring, so you’ll need to make sure you have enough savings to cover them as well.

“We rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people,” Ame says.

Some bills are monthly, others come once a year

If you live in rented accommodation, you may have to pay service costs, which can range from around €50 to over €250 a month if you live in a building with a lift and lots of amenities such as co-working spaces or a gym. The monthly service fee is an estimate, and you will get a final invoice once a year. Rents also go up once a year, usually in July, by a percentage set by the government. For 2027, the increase in the non-rent-controlled sector, where most expats live, will be 4.4%.

You can keep an eye on your gas and electricity bills if you have a smart meter. If you pay too little to cover your usage, you will be invoiced for the extra costs and your monthly payment is likely to increase. If you pay too much, you’ll get the difference back.

“All this means that you need to really plan out your spending over the year,” says ABN Amro expert Ame. “For example, if you have the 30% ruling, will you still be able to meet your payments when it ends in five years’ time?”

Once you understand the costs you face, create a budget that includes fixed spending, savings and fun stuff. Remember to adjust it if your financial situation changes.

Why is banking in the Netherlands different?

“It’s important to explain to new arrivals how the financial system works in the Netherlands, because it may be very different to back home,” says Ame. “For example, we rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people from countries where they use a credit card as part of their regular spending.”

You’ll need a Dutch bank account for your salary, your rent and pretty much everything else. The Netherlands runs on digital payments, with debit cards, internet payments and payment request apps dominating how the Dutch spend their money.

“If I ask people how much they spend on rent or groceries, they often give a round number – €100 or €200 – but in practice it is more than that,” says Ame. “Once you are aware of what is really happening in your finances, you will understand how much you can actually spend each month.”

How can you improve your financial fitness?

What to know more about how to stay financially fit in the Netherlands. Join ABN Amro’s free webinar on Wednesday, 28 October, 12:00–13:00 CET. Register now

item.title: Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
item.description:
Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.

The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.

Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.

Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.

Idriss Ghazi Kareem

Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.

The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.

Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The  Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.

“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”

The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.

Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.

“Floating coffins”

Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”

And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

item.title: Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
item.description:
Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.

The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.

Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.

The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.

When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.

The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.

Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”

Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

item.title: Lost Erasmus book returns to Rotterdam after 400 years
item.description:
Lost Erasmus book returns to Rotterdam after 400 years

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A book by Dutch Renaissance philosopher Desiderius Erasmus, which was thought to be lost, has been returned to Rotterdam after being identified by a collector in the US.

La civilité puérile (The Civility of Children) is a short collection of thoughts on good manners in children, printed in French in 1609.

The booklet contains rules such as: “It is downright ridiculous to make trumpet sounds with your nose: leave that to horn players and elephants.”

“If someone else sneezes, you must wish them good health (pay close attention to that)” is another piece of advice, along with “only sit down at the table after you have washed your hands, and cut your nails too.”

John Tholen, a curator at the Rotterdam Library, told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that getting the book back after four centuries was a very special event.

“We have found an unknown piece of the puzzle regarding the history and influence of Erasmus’s ideas,” Tholen said. “This copy is the only one left in the world from a print run of perhaps as many as 1,000.”

The UNESCO Erasmus Collection in Rotterdam holds more than 3,000 editions of the scholar’s works, plus another 3,000 books and articles about him published after 1900.

item.title: Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train
item.description:
Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The iconic Apekop train, officially known as Mat ’64 (Materieel ’64), made its last journey on Wednesday before heading back into retirement.

Originally retired from service in 2016, the passenger train was brought back by operator Keolis last year, to the delight of train enthusiasts, to run between Amersfoort and Barneveld Zuid after refurbishment work on newer trains led to a rolling stock shortage.

But its 12.25pm departure from Barneveld Zuid on Wednesday is said to be its final trip. The train will now return to Stichting 2454CRW, a volunteer organisation that maintains old trains.

First appearing on Dutch tracks in 1961, the Mat ’64, the last NS train built largely in the Netherlands, came to symbolise Dutch commuter travel. The trains served passengers for more than five decades, with hundreds in service at their peak.

The nickname Apekop, which translates as “monkey head”, comes from the train’s distinctive rounded nose.
